0.note: **For the chief musician** is an instruction about who should lead people in singing or playing music with this psalm. This could refer to the person in charge of music for temple worship. If your readers would not be familiar with this role, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the worship leader]
See how you translated the expression “on Jeduthun” in the superscription to Psalm 39.

1.note: Asaph is repeating the expression **my voice is to God** in order to intensify his expression of crying out to God. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I earnestly cry out to God] or [I cry out with my voice again and again to God]

Here, **My voice** represents Asaph’s act of calling out to God in prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My prayer]

2.note: Asaph is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At the time of my trouble] or [When I was in trouble]

Here, **my hand was stretched out** was a symbolic action by which Asaph showed his persistent prayer and pleading to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I lifted my hands to God in continual prayer]

Asaph is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to represent all of him in his refusal of comfort. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I refused to be comforted]

3.q: אֶזְכְּרָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְ⁠אֶֽהֱמָיָ֑ה אָשִׂ֓יחָה ׀ וְ⁠תִתְעַטֵּ֖ף רוּחִ֣⁠י
3.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [I remembered God and groaned; yes, my spirit grew faint as I meditated]

Here, **spirit** represents Asaph’s inner strength or vitality. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I felt weak] or [and I became exhausted]

4.note: Asaph is speaking of God preventing him from sleeping as if God **held the lids of my eyes** open. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You prevented me from sleeping] or [You kept me awake]

5.note: These two phrases **days from antiquity** and **years of long ago** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [times long, long ago]

Here, **days** represents a particular period of time in the past. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time long ago] or [the era of antiquity]

6.note: Asaph is speaking of **my heart** as if it were the place where thinking and reflection occur. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I meditate within myself] or [I reflect deeply]

Asaph is using one part of a person, his **spirit**, to mean all of him in the act of searching for understanding. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I search diligently]

7.q: הַֽ֭⁠לְ⁠עוֹלָמִים יִזְנַ֥ח ׀ אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י וְ⁠לֹֽא־יֹסִ֖יף לִ⁠רְצ֣וֹת עֽוֹד
7.note: Asaph is using the question form to express his distress and uncertainty. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [The Lord will surely not reject me forever! He will show me favor again!] or [I am afraid that the Lord will reject me forever and will never again show me favor.]

Asaph is using **again add** as a common expression to mean “continue.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And will he not continue to show favor] or [And will he not ever show favor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will he … treat me favorably] or [will he … be favorable toward me]

8.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his faithfulness to his covenant] or [his faithful commitment to his covenant]

Asaph is using **for generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “throughout all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [throughout all generations]

8.q: הֶ⁠אָפֵ֣ס לָ⁠נֶ֣צַח חַסְדּ֑⁠וֹ גָּ֥מַר אֹ֝֗מֶר לְ⁠דֹ֣ר וָ⁠דֹֽר
8.note: Asaph is using the question form to express his deep sorrow and fear that God has abandoned him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Your covenant faithfulness must be gone forever! Your promise must have failed forever!] or [Surely your covenant faithfulness is gone forever. Surely your promise has failed forever.]

9.q: הֲ⁠שָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל אִם־קָפַ֥ץ בְּ֝⁠אַ֗ף רַחֲמָ֥י⁠ו
9.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Has God forgotten to be gracious and shut up his compassions in his nose]

Asaph speaks of anger as if it were a person shutting a door to keep another person, compassion, from coming out. Alternate translation: [has God stopped showing us compassion because he is angry with us]

9.q: הֲ⁠שָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל אִם־קָפַ֥ץ בְּ֝⁠אַ֗ף רַחֲמָ֥י⁠ו סֶֽלָה
9.note: Asaph is using the question form to express his anguish and doubt, not to seek information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [God has forgotten to be gracious. He has shut off his compassion in anger.] or [Surely God has not forgotten to be gracious! Surely his anger has not shut off his compassion!]

Asaph is speaking of God’s **compassions** as if they were something physical that his anger could **shut up**, like closing a door or stopping a flow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has his anger caused him to withhold his compassion] or [has he withheld his compassion because of his anger]
Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his anger]

10.note: This could mean: (1) Asaph was speaking to himself or (2) Asaph was speaking to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And I said to myself] or [And I said to Yahweh]

Asaph is speaking of his great distress as if it were a physical **wounding**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This is my great distress] or [This is what afflicts me]

Here, **the right hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power] or [the strength]

11.note: Here, **from antiquity** represents the distant past when God did his remarkable deeds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the wonders you did long ago] or [your wonderful deeds in ancient times]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonder**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wonderful things that you did long ago]

12.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And I will ponder and meditate on all your deeds]

13.note: Asaph is speaking of God’s manner of acting as if it were a **way** or path that he travels. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God, the manner in which you act is holy] or [God, everything you do is holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a holy way] or [is a way that is holy]

Asaph is using the question form to emphasize that no god compares to the true God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no god is great like God] or [there is no god as great as God!]

14.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how strong you are] or [how powerfully you act]

15.note: Here, **arm** represents God’s power and ability to rescue. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your power] or [with your mighty strength]

Asaph is speaking of the later Israelites as if they were actually the **sons of Jacob and Joseph**. He means that they are the descendants of these ancestors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob and Joseph] or [the people descended from Jacob and Joseph]

16.note: Asaph is repeating the phrase **the waters saw you** in order to intensify his expression of the idea it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [The waters surely saw you, God]

16.q: רָ֘א֤וּ⁠ךָ מַּ֨יִם ׀ אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים רָא֣וּ⁠ךָ מַּ֣יִם יָחִ֑ילוּ אַ֝֗ף יִרְגְּז֥וּ תְהֹמֽוֹת
16.note: Starting in this verse and extending through verse 19, Asaph is speaking of God’s powerful actions during the exodus as if they were a storm, with **thunder** representing God’s voice, **arrows** and **lightning** representing God’s power striking out, and **the waters** and **the earth** reacting in fear by trembling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express these images with a comparison or state the meaning plainly.

Asaph is speaking of **the waters** as if they were living things that could see and respond with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When you, God, came to the waters, they moved back in fear] or [The waters moved away from you, God, as if they saw you]

These two phrases, **they trembled** and **the depths shook**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and they trembled, even the depths shook]

17.note: By **gave a sound**, Asaph means that the skies thundered. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the skies thundered]

Asaph is speaking of lightning bolts as if they were **arrows** that God shot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your lightning bolts also flashed in all directions] or [you also shot lightning across the sky]

18.note: Asaph is speaking of the sound of God’s thunder as if it were **in the whirlwind** and as if God’s voice or presence were speaking from within the storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your voice thundered from the whirlwind] or [You spoke with thundering power in the storm]

The terms **trembled** and **shook** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [shook violently] or [quaked greatly]

19.note: Asaph is speaking of God’s actions and guidance as if they were a **way** and **path** that he traveled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your deeds were done in the sea and your works] or [You acted in the sea, and you worked]

These two phrases, **Your way went through the sea** and **your path through many waters**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Your way went through the sea, yes, your path went through many waters]

Asaph is speaking of God as if he were a person who could leave **footprints** when walking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but no trace of your presence could be seen] or [but there was no sign of where you had been]

The expression **your footprints were not discerned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but no one could discern your footprints] or [but your footprints could not be seen]

20.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd leads and cares for **a flock**, so God led and cared for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as a shepherd leads a flock] or [with the care and guidance of a shepherd]

Here, **hand** represents agency and leadership. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [through the leadership of Moses and Aaron] or [by means of Moses and Aaron]
